title: Safety and Efficacy of Riluzole in Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study (RISCIS): A Multi-Center, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Double-Blinded Trial
article_subtype: International, multicenter, prospective, adaptive, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III trial
condition_or_topic: Acute cervical traumatic spinal cord injury (tSCI) and treatment with riluzole.
clinical_background: tSCI has substantial consequences for patients, families, and healthcare systems, with estimated annual incidence ranging from 10 to 85 per million individuals worldwide. No pharmacological treatment has yet been identified that is both safe and effective at improving neurological and functional outcomes; trials of methylprednisolone and GM-1 ganglioside have yielded suggestive but equivocal evidence of benefit. Riluzole inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels and reduces excitotoxic glutamate release after tSCI. Pre-clinical studies found reduced secondary tissue injury, while a Phase I/IIa pilot study supported an acceptable safety profile and suggested possible treatment benefit.
objectives: Evaluate the efficacy and safety of riluzole in acute cervical tSCI, with change in Upper Extremity Motor (UEM) scores at 180 days as the primary efficacy end-point.
Assess secondary neurological, functional, quality-of-life, and pain outcomes, including outcomes within baseline AIS grade subgroups.
clinical_question: In patients aged 18-75 with cervical (C4-C8) tSCI, AIS grades A-C, who can receive treatment within the first 12h of injury, does riluzole, given as 100 mg twice per day (BID) for the first 24h followed by 50mg BID for the following 13 days, compared with placebo, improve Upper Extremity Motor (UEM) scores at 180 days, improve secondary neurological and functional outcomes, and have an acceptable safety profile?
interpretation: The primary comparison favored riluzole for Upper Extremity Motor recovery at 180 days but did not meet the prespecified threshold for statistical significance; the authors therefore cannot establish its efficacy. Other neurological and functional outcomes generally favored riluzole, with potentially meaningful findings in prespecified AIS subgroups, particularly those with incomplete cervical injuries. In the AIS B subgroup, the 18-point difference in SCIM improvement exceeded the cited 10-point threshold for substantial clinical improvement, although differences in injury level between groups may partly explain that result. The authors found no evidence of serious adverse events attributed to riluzole.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors relate these findings to preclinical work and an earlier Phase I/IIa study that suggested benefit and supported riluzole’s safety in traumatic spinal cord injury. They also cite a pharmacodynamic investigation linking riluzole to lower phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain (pNF-H) levels than placebo and associating its concentration with neurological recovery after 6 months. They note that estimates of a clinically important motor-score change have evolved since the trial was designed, but state that the present findings have not been replicated or externally validated.
clinical_implications: The subgroup findings suggest a possible neurological and functional benefit from riluzole in acute cervical traumatic spinal cord injury, but do not establish efficacy.
The apparent safety profile may be relevant when weighing a possible benefit in an uncommon condition without an accepted effective neuroprotective or neuroregenerative treatment.
Functional gains may matter to patients even when overall motor scores do not capture their effect on quality of life.
practice_implications: The authors suggest that guideline committees review the trial’s secondary findings to clarify whether riluzole has a role in managing traumatic spinal cord injury; they do not make a definitive treatment recommendation.
limitations: Pandemic-related early termination left recruitment at 55% of the planned sample size, limiting interpretation of whether the prespecified superiority criterion was met.
The cohort consisted predominantly of AIS A and upper cervical injuries, which the authors describe as having less potential for recovery.

A greater proportion of higher-level injuries in the AIS B placebo group may partly account for the SCIM difference through respiratory-management scores, although self-care also improved significantly with riluzole.
Neurological examination in the acute stage has limitations, and a broadly applicable minimally clinically important difference remains difficult to define.
The findings have not been replicated or externally validated.
strengths: The design and analysis plan were preregistered, and participants were assigned through block randomization to groups that the authors describe as comparable at baseline.
Investigators assessed primary outcomes while blinded to treatment allocation.
The authors evaluated prespecified primary and subgroup analyses alongside additional sensitivity analyses.
open_questions: Whether riluzole improves neurological or functional recovery sufficiently to establish efficacy in acute cervical traumatic spinal cord injury remains unresolved.
The appropriate minimally clinically important difference and the most informative primary outcome for traumatic spinal cord injury trials remain uncertain.
Whether objective imaging or chemical biomarkers, including pNF-H, can reliably indicate neurological recovery requires validation.
future_directions: Further investigate the neurological and functional findings, including the secondary outcomes across AIS subgroups.
Examine the use of functional measures such as SCIM in primary trial analyses and study how neuroprotective or regenerative agents affect functional recovery and rehabilitation.
Validate biomarkers of neurological recovery, including pNF-H, for future trials.

Explore more personalized, patient-centered trial outcomes and innovative designs, including multi-arm, multi-stage platforms, to address recruitment and cost challenges in traumatic spinal cord injury research.
study_design: International, prospective, multi-center, adaptive Phase III trial with block randomization in a 1:1 ratio, double blinding, and a placebo control. The sponsor suspended enrollment on May 1, 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic and terminated the trial in April 2021 independently of the interim analysis results.

population.description: Participants with acute cervical traumatic spinal cord injury (tSCI) recruited at 21 clinical sites in North America and Australia. The trial enrolled 193 participants. Two participants found after randomization to have a C3 injury were retained in the analysis; a participant found to have a T1 injury was lost to follow-up and excluded from the final analysis.
inclusion_criteria: Neurological Level of Injury between C4-C8 and an initial post-arrival International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI) assessment showing American Spinal Cord Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS) grade ‘‘A,’’ ‘‘B,’’ or ‘‘C’’.
Presentation to a participating hospital and ability to receive the study drug within the first 12h after injury.
Signed informed consent before screening procedures.
population.mean_age: Riluzole group: 49.4 years (SD=17.1); control group: 47.6 years (SD=16.0).
population.care_setting: Participating hospitals; follow-up visits were preferably conducted in outpatient clinics, with an examiner visiting participants who could not attend.

interventions: Riluzole 100mg at enrollment (0h) and 12h, followed by 50mg every 12h for the next 13 days. Other medical care and the type and timing of surgery were left to the treating physicians; investigators agreed on early surgery within 24h and adherence to existing tSCI management guidelines.
comparators: Placebo capsules: two capsules at 0h and 12h, followed by one capsule every 12h for the next 13 days.

primary: Change from baseline in Upper Extremity Motor (UEM) score at 180 days; this replaced change in total motor (TOTM) score before unblinding and analysis.
secondary: Change in AIS grade, which replaced the ISNCSCI sensory component as a secondary efficacy endpoint.
Changes in ISNCSCI TOTM, sensory and Lower Extremity Motor (LEM) scores.
Spinal Cord Independence Measure (SCIM) at 180 days relative to baseline.

Changes between baseline and 180 days in Short Form 36 Version 2 (SF-36v2 ), European Quality of Life 5 Dimensions 3 Level Version health utility, Graded Redefined Assessment of Strength Sensibility and Prehension (GRASSP), and self-reported Numeric Pain Rating Scale (pain NRS) scores.
Adverse events, classified with MeDRA Version 14.1 and summarized by system organ class, preferred term, severity, relationship to study drug, outcome, action taken, and time to event.

statistical_methods: Primary efficacy analyses used both an intent-to-treat (ITT) population, with missing 180-day values imputed, and a completed cases (CC) population with a 180-day efficacy measurement. Safety analyses used a modified ITT population of consenting participants who received at least one study-treatment dose and had follow-up. A one-sided superiority test assessed whether the riluzole–placebo difference exceeded 0, with alpha=0.025; secondary outcomes also underwent one-sided superiority testing using appropriate methods. A pre-planned subgroup analysis examined 180-day motor-score changes by baseline AIS grade ‘‘A,’’ ‘‘B,’’ and ‘‘C’’. Table 2 reports one-tailed t-tests for motor-score comparisons. Post hoc sensitivity approaches included multivariate linear regression, analysis of covariance and binary-outcome analyses. Analyses were performed in RStudio version 1.4.1103. The article reports an original estimated sample size of 316, revised to 324 when the interim design changed to a non-binding futility hypothesis; its abstract also reports planned enrollment of 351. The pre-specified calculation of 156 per group provided power of 0.90 to detect an effect size of 9 in total motor score change.
follow_up: The principal assessment was at 180 days; a 365-day visit was planned, but some participants did not reach it before study completion.

main_findings.description: The trial ended before reaching its planned enrollment, and the primary efficacy analysis did not meet the prespecified criterion for riluzole superiority.
main_findings.context: Enrollment represented 54.9% of the planned 351 patients according to the abstract; the results section describes it as 55% of the pre-planned sample size. Participants were enrolled at 21 clinical sites across North America and Australia.

main_findings.description: In the completed-cases analysis, riluzole produced a greater mean improvement than placebo in the primary Upper Extremity Motor outcome at 180 days, but the difference was not statistically significant.

main_findings.description: The imputed intention-to-treat analysis also did not establish superiority for riluzole on the primary Upper Extremity Motor outcome at 180 days.

main_findings.context: Intention to Treat- Imputed data (N: 188); mean change was 15.59 among 94 riluzole recipients and 14.35 among 94 placebo recipients.

main_findings.metric: difference in mean change, riluzole versus placebo
main_findings.context: Mean change was 17.55 among 65 riluzole recipients and 16.10 among 68 placebo recipients.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Riluzole: 96 (100.0) participants had 1722 adverse events; placebo: 97 (100.0) participants had 1786 adverse events.
safety_results.discontinuations: Discontinuation of study medication due to adverse events: riluzole 0 participants and 0 events; placebo 0 participants and 0 events.
notable_adverse_events: Death: riluzole 9 (9.78) participants and 9 events, Wilson confidence interval 0.05-0.17; control 10 (9.52) participants and 10 events, Wilson confidence interval 0.05-0.18. The article does not attribute these deaths to treatment.

Serious adverse events: riluzole 51 (53.1) participants and 110 events, Wilson confidence interval 0.06-0.09; control 52 (53.6) participants and 132 events. The article reports no serious adverse events related to riluzole.

Resolved adverse events: riluzole 92 (95.8) participants and 1204 events; control 92 (94.8) participants and 1,195 events. The results prose reports resolution of 69.9% (1,204) of riluzole-group events and 66.9% (1,195) of placebo-group events.
Adverse events resolved with residual effects: riluzole 37 (38.5) participants and 77 events; control 34 (35.1) participants and 108 events.
Unresolved adverse events: riluzole 78 (81.3) participants and 349 events; control 75 (77.3) participants and 405 events.
Adverse events with unknown outcome: riluzole 27 (28.1) participants and 81 events; control 25 (25.8) participants and 65 events.
Liver enzyme elevation at 14 days did not differ statistically significantly between riluzole and placebo.

subgroup_analyses: In the AIS A subgroup, mean neurological levels gained at 180 days were 0.50 with riluzole versus 0.12 with placebo; the abstract reports a difference of 0.38, CI: -0.2-0.9, while the discussion reports p: 0.077.

In the AIS B subgroup, SCIM gain at 180 days was 45.3 with riluzole versus 27.3 with placebo, with a reported difference of 18.0, CI: -1.7-38.0. The gains chiefly involved self-care, respiration, and sphincter management.

For AIS B, the results section reports mean SF-36 mental component score change at 180 days of 1.6 with riluzole versus -11.6 with placebo. The abstract separately reports Short Form 36 mental health domain change of 2.01 versus -11.58, with d: 13.2 CI: 1.2-24.8. The discussion characterizes the AIS B mental-score change as statistically superior with riluzole.

For AIS B, EQ5 Health Status score change at 180 days was -12.1 with riluzole versus -29.7 with placebo; the reported difference was 17.6, CI: 1.2-24.8. The discussion characterizes the AIS B health-status change as statistically superior with riluzole.

In post hoc multivariate linear regression for the AIS C subgroup, riluzole versus placebo was associated with increased Upper Motor score change from baseline at 180 days; the results section reports standard error [SE] 8.0 and CI 1.5-14.4. For Total Motor score change, it reports SE 13.8 and CI 3.1-24.5. The abstract assigns those numerical pairs to total motor and upper extremity motor scores, respectively, rather than to the outcomes named in the results section.
The discussion describes statistically significant Upper Motor and Total Motor changes in the AIS C multivariate analyses, but no significant change in total SCIM score for AIS C.

The authors describe neurological and functional improvements across the AIS A, AIS B, and AIS C subgroups in secondary analyses, while noting that motor and functional improvements tended to be greater in the incomplete AIS B and AIS C cohorts.
secondary_results: SCIM gain at 180 days averaged 33.9 points with riluzole and 27.8 points with placebo.

Mean AIS grade change at 180 days was 0.98 with riluzole and 1.00 with placebo. Improvement by one or more AIS grades occurred in 48 riluzole recipients (73.85%) and 45 placebo recipients (66.18%); p: 0.335.
Mean neurological levels gained at 180 days were 1.2 with riluzole versus 0.4 with placebo; difference: 0.8 with 95% CI -0.5-2.0.
SF36 mental score change at 180 days was -3.0 with riluzole versus -5.2 with placebo; D: 2.2 CI: -8.3-13.2.
SF36 physical component score change at 180 days was -23.5 with riluzole versus -25.5 with placebo; d: 2.0 CI:-2.3-6.2.
EuroQol 5-Dimension (EQ5D) Health State change at 180 days was -14.9 with riluzole versus -17.4 with placebo; d: 2.5 CI: -8.25-13.2.
At 180 days, treatment groups did not differ statistically significantly in changes in total pinprick score, sensory score, or GRASSP strength and sensation scores.
Post hoc covariance and binary-outcome sensitivity analyses did not alter the conclusions of the primary efficacy analysis.

The discussion cites a separate pharmacodynamic investigation that associated riluzole administration with lower phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain (pNF-H) than placebo and found a positive correlation between riluzole concentration and neurological recovery after 6 months; these are attributed to that investigation, not presented as efficacy endpoints of this trial.

main_conclusion: RISCIS did not meet its prespecified primary efficacy criterion for Riluzole in acute cervical traumatic spinal cord injury; premature termination and recruitment below target limit a definitive efficacy conclusion. Secondary analyses suggested neurological and functional gains in AIS subgroups, without serious adverse events attributed to the drug, and the authors consider further investigation and guideline review warranted.
narrative_summary: RISCIS assessed Riluzole for acute cervical traumatic spinal cord injury in an international, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial. Eligible participants had AIS A-C injuries and could begin treatment within 12h. The Riluzole regimen was 100mg at enrollment and 12h, followed by 50mg every 12h for the next 13 days. The primary endpoint was Upper Extremity Motor score change at 180 days. Recruitment stopped during the COVID-19 pandemic after 193 participants had enrolled, below the planned sample size. In complete cases, mean gains were 16.42 with Riluzole and 14.65 with placebo; the difference was 1.76 (95% CI: -2.54-6.06; p Value 0.2093), so the primary efficacy criterion was not met. Prespecified subgroup assessments suggested functional or neurological improvement across AIS grades A, B and C. In AIS B, the reported SCIM gain was 45.3 with Riluzole versus 27.3 with placebo; in AIS A, mean neurological levels gained were 0.50 versus 0.12. The authors also describe motor-score improvements in AIS C, while cautioning that efficacy cannot be established definitively. Safety analyses found no serious adverse events attributed to Riluzole and no discontinuations of study medication because of adverse events. Given the shortfall in recruitment and the absence of an accepted neuroprotective treatment, the authors propose further study and consideration of the secondary findings by guideline groups.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Riluzole antagonizes sodium-glutamate activity, reduces neurodegeneration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and had shown encouraging recovery findings in pre-clinical traumatic spinal cord injury (tSCI) models and early clinical trials. This international, multi-center, prospective, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, adaptive Phase III trial (NCT01597518) assessed its efficacy and safety in acute cervical tSCI. Patients with American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS) A-C injury at C4-C8, treated <12h after injury, received oral riluzole 100 mg twice per day (BID) for the first 24h and 50mg BID for the following 13 days, or placebo. The primary efficacy measure was change in Upper Extremity Motor (UEM) scores at 180 days, analyzed in intention to treat (ITT) and completed cases (CC) populations. Planned enrollment was 351 patients. Recruitment began in October 2013, stopped in May 2020 during the global COVID-19 pandemic, and the trial ended in April 2021. Randomization included 193 patients, or 54.9% of planned enrollment; follow-up at 180 days was 82.7%. Among CC participants at 180 days, the riluzole-minus-placebo difference in mean gain was 1.76 UEM scores (95% confidence interval: -2.54-6.06) and 2.86 total motor scores (CI: -6.79-12.52). No serious adverse events attributed to riluzole were identified. The abstract reports that pre-planned sensitivity analyses in AIS C found improvements in total motor scores (estimate: standard error [SE] 8.0; CI 1.5-14.4) and upper extremity motor scores (SE 13.8; CI 3.1-24.5) at 6 months; its assignment of those estimates differs from the Results section. In AIS B, Spinal Cord Independence Measure scores were 45.3 versus 27.3 (d: 18.0 CI: -1.7-38.0), and Short Form 36 mental health domain changes were 2.01 versus -11.58 (d: 13.2 CI: 1.2-24.8) at 180 days. In AIS A, mean neurological-level gains at 6 months were 0.50 with riluzole and 0.12 with placebo (d: 0.38, CI: -0.2-0.9). The primary efficacy criterion was not met, possibly because of inadequate statistical power. The authors report significant functional-recovery gains in pre-planned secondary analyses across cervical SCI subgroups AIS grades A, B and C. They suggest further investigation and consideration by guideline groups of the possible clinical relevance of secondary outcomes, given the absence of an accepted neuroprotective treatment for this uncommon orphan disorder.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Traumatic spinal cord injury (tSCI) substantially affects injured people, their families, and healthcare systems. Estimated annual incidence varies geographically from 10 to 85 per million individuals. No pharmacological treatment has yet been established as both safe and effective for improving neurological and functional outcomes after tSCI. Trials of methylprednisolone in National Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study [NASCIS] II and III and of GM-1 ganglioside yielded indications of possible benefit that remained equivocal. Riluzole is a sodium-channel-blocking benzothiazole anticonvulsant. Following tSCI, it may preserve neuronal ionic balance and reduce release of excitotoxic glutamate. It is widely used for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which involves progressive degeneration of motor neurons and corticospinal tracts, and is approved by the U. S. Food and Drug Administration for chronic ALS treatment. Potent neurotoxic or cardiotoxic effects are not characteristic of riluzole, although reversible hepatotoxicity has been reported. Pre-clinical tSCI studies provide strong evidence that riluzole limits the secondary-injury cascade and consequent tissue destruction in animals. After injury, increased membrane permeability and synaptic glutamate release prolong postsynaptic excitation, contributing to neuronal edema and death. Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels by riluzole reduces glutamate release and may limit this excitotoxicity. The North American Clinical Trial Network published the trial rationale beforehand. A multi-center Phase I/IIa pilot in tSCI examined riluzole safety and pharmacokinetics. Its 12-h treatment window and 2-week course were selected to coincide with glutamatergic excitotoxicity, described as lasting from several minutes after injury until 2 weeks after injury. Enteral riluzole pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in tSCI had also been established before this trial. The pilot supported acceptable safety, suggested possible treatment benefit, and showed that a larger efficacy trial was feasible.

document_sections.heading: Methods Eligibility and recruitment
document_sections.content: People presenting to a participating hospital with acute cervical tSCI within 12h of injury were screened after signing an Informed Consent Document. Eligibility considered ages 18-75 (inclusive), a Neurological Level of Injury from C4-C8, American Spinal Cord Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS) grade ‘‘A,’’ ‘‘B,’’ or ‘‘C’’ on the first International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI) examination after arrival, and the ability to start investigational treatment within the first 12h after injury. Table S1 contains the complete inclusion and exclusion criteria. Allocation to riluzole or placebo used a 1:1 ratio.

document_sections.heading: Study intervention
document_sections.content: The riluzole arm received 100mg at enrollment (0h) and at 12h, designated doses 1 and 2, followed by 50mg every 12h for the next 13 days, designated doses 3-28. The placebo arm received two capsules at 0h and 12h, then one capsule every 12h for the next 13 days, on the corresponding dose schedule. Attending physicians determined other medical care and the type and timing of surgery. Investigators nevertheless agreed on early surgery within 24h and adherence to existing tSCI management guidelines.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up evaluation
document_sections.content: Study personnel trained in the protocol and ISNCSCI examinations performed assessments. Outpatient visits were preferred, but an investigator or designated examiner could visit a participant unable to attend the clinic. Telephone and mail data collection were prohibited. Table S2 outlines treatment and assessments by scheduled visit. The study continued until the last enrolled participant reached 180-day follow-up, so some participants had no 365-day visit.

document_sections.heading: Study end-points
document_sections.content: Before unblinding or analysis, investigators changed the primary efficacy end-point at 180 days from total motor (TOTM) score change to Upper Extremity Motor (UEM) score change, citing subsequent evidence that UEM better focuses assessment on hand and arm control. They also replaced the ISNCSCI sensory component among secondary efficacy end-points with AIS grade change because they considered sensory scores insufficiently useful and reliable for tSCI classification. ISNCSCI TOTM and sensory scores remained secondary measures of possible efficacy. Other secondary measures were Spinal Cord Independence Measure (SCIM) at 180 days relative to baseline and baseline-to-180-day changes in ISNCSCI sensory scores, Lower Extremity Motor (LEM) scores, Short Form 36 Version 2 (SF-36v2 ), European Quality of Life 5 Dimensions 3 Level Version health utility, Graded Redefined Assessment of Strength Sensibility and Prehension (GRASSP), and self-reported Numeric Pain Rating Scale (pain NRS) scores. Adverse events were coded with MeDRA Version 14.1 and summarized by treatment arm, system organ class, preferred term, severity, relationship to study drug, outcome, action taken, and time-to-event.

document_sections.heading: Analysis samples/population
document_sections.content: The original estimated sample size was 316. All international participating sites followed the same monitored and validated protocol, and their data were analyzed as one cohort. Primary analyses used both intentto-treat (ITT) and completed cases (CC) populations. ITT comprised randomized participants who received at least one investigational-product dose; missing 180-day values were imputed, using a method described in the Supplementary Material. CC comprised participants who received at least one treatment dose and had an efficacy measurement at 180-day follow-up. Safety analyses used a modified ITT population of consenting participants who received at least one study-directed dose and had any follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Statistical analysis
document_sections.content: The prespecified success criterion was superiority of riluzole over placebo. A single one-sided test evaluated a null hypothesis that the treatment-arm difference was equal to or less than 0; rejecting it would support superiority. Statistical significance used alpha=0.025. Secondary outcomes used appropriate methods and one-sided superiority tests. A pre-planned subgroup analysis examined 180-day motor-score changes according to baseline AIS groups ‘‘A,’’ ‘‘B,’’ and ‘‘C.’’ Analyses were performed in RStudio version 1.4.1103.

document_sections.heading: Interim analysis and stopping rules
document_sections.content: The sponsor stopped enrollment on May 1, 2020, during the global COVID pandemic, after enrollment of 193 participants. Because enrollment was approaching the protocol's planned interim-analysis sample size (60%), the Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) recommended an interim analysis. Its independent statistician recommended replacing the original sequential design with rejection under a non-binding futility hypothesis (H1), allowing review of several sensitivity analyses instead of reliance on one binding decision. This increased the sample size from 316 to 324. A recommendation to end the study was intended if statistical success was achieved or the futility boundary was reached; Tables S3 and S4 provide the thresholds and revised sequential-design parameters. The sponsor's decision to terminate the trial in April 2021 reflected concern about in-person exposure of patients and research staff, alongside uncertainty about conducting clinical research during the COVID-19 pandemic. It was independent of DSMB recommendations and interim findings.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: From October of 2013 until the sponsor, AO Spine North America/ AOSNA, suspended screening and enrollment on May 1, 2020, the study enrolled 193 participants, reported here as 55% of the planned sample, at 21 sites in North America and Australia. Post-randomization review found two participants with C3 injuries; despite the protocol deviation, both remained in the analysis. Another participant was found on review to have a T1 injury, was lost to follow-up, and was excluded from the final analysis. Follow-up was 82.7% (139 participants) at 180 days and 82.4% (131 participants) at 365 days, with similar rates between treatment arms. At 180 days, visits were attended by 69 of 81 (85.19%) expected riluzole participants and 70 of 87 (80.46%) expected placebo participants. The participant flow is depicted in Figure 1. Table 1 presents demographic and injury characteristics by arm: mean age was 49.4 years (standard deviation [SD]=17.1, range 19-74 years) in the treatment arm, with 17 females and 79 males, and 47.6 years (SD=16.0, range 2074 years) in the control arm, with 18 females and 79 males. AIS A was the most common baseline grade, affecting 49 or 51.58% of riluzole patients and 52 or 53.61% of placebo patients. AIS B comprised 19 patients in each arm, and AIS C comprised 26 patients in each arm. Surgical decompression within 24h was received by 94.62% of participants. In the CC primary analysis at 180 days, riluzole produced a higher mean UEM gain than placebo, 16.4 versus 14.7; the between-arm difference of 1.8 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -2.5-6.1) was not statistically significant. Other CC motor-score gains also favored riluzole without reaching significance: TOTM was 34.0 versus 31.1 (d: 2.86 CI: -6.8-12.5), and LEM was 17.6 versus 16.1 (d: 1.45 CI: -4.8-7.7). Table 2 presents motor-score means, participant counts, between-arm differences, confidence intervals, and p values for CC and imputed ITT analyses at 180 days. For prespecified secondary outcomes, mean SCIM gain at 180 days was 33.9 with riluzole versus 27.8 with placebo. Mean AIS grade changes were 0.98 and 1.00, respectively; at least one AIS-grade improvement occurred in 48 riluzole patients (73.85%) and 45 placebo patients (66.18%; p: 0.335). Table S6 details AIS changes, and Table S7 gives motor-score changes by time point. Most other prespecified measures also showed larger average gains with riluzole at 180 days: neurological levels, 1.2 versus 0.4 (difference: 0.8 with 95% CI -0.5-2.0); SF36 mental score change, -3.0 versus -5.2 (D: 2.2 CI: -8.3-13.2); physical component change, -23.5 versus -25.5 (d: 2.0 CI:-2.3-6.2); and EuroQol 5-Dimension (EQ5D) Health State change, -14.9 versus -17.4 (d: 2.5 CI: -8.25-13.2). Between-arm differences in total pinprick, sensory scores, and GRASSP strength and sensation change at 180 days were not statistically significant. Among AIS A participants, mean neurological-level gain at 180 days was 0.50 with riluzole versus 0.12 with placebo. Figure S1 shows baseline-to-180-day motor changes by AIS subgroup. In AIS B, riluzole versus placebo produced an SF-36 mental component mean gain of 1.6 versus -11.6 at 180 days, SCIM gain of 45.3 versus 27.3 (d: 18.0 CI: -1.7-38.0), and EQ5 Health Status change of -12.1 versus -29.7 (d: 17.6 CI: 1.2-24.8). AIS B SCIM improvement was concentrated mainly in selfcare, respiration, and sphincter management. For AIS C, post hoc multivariate linear regression associated riluzole, relative to placebo, with greater baseline-to-180-day change in Upper Motor (standard error [SE] 8.0; CI 1.5-14.4) and Total Motor (SE 13.8; CI 3.1-24.5) scores. Table S8 contains the full model results. Table 3 summarizes adverse events: riluzole recipients had 1722 adverse events (AEs) among 96 participants, 110 serious adverse events (SAEs) among 51 participants, and nine deaths; placebo recipients had 1786 AEs among 97 participants, 132 SAEs among 52 participants according to the table, and 10 deaths. The Results prose gives the placebo SAE participant count as 132, whereas Table 3 gives 52. Resolved AEs numbered 1,204 (69.9%) with riluzole and 1,195 (66.9%) with placebo. No participant discontinued study medication because of an AE. Table S9 categorizes AEs by disease, and Table S10 shows no statistically significant between-arm difference in liver-enzyme elevation at 14 days. Post hoc covariance models and binary-outcome approaches, provided in Figure S2 and Table S11, did not alter the primary conclusions.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The sponsor ended RISCIS early because of the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors cite an estimate that the pandemic caused 2043 clinical trials to be suspended or terminated, affecting 4 million prospective participants. They found no evidence of serious adverse events attributable to riluzole. Mean UEM gain at 180 days exceeded placebo but did not meet statistical-significance criteria. Recovery trends also favored riluzole across other ISNCSCI motor measures, neurological-level gain, SCIM, SF-36, and EQ5D Health Status change. In the AIS B subgroup (n: 29), the 18-point between-arm difference in total SCIM gain exceeded a cited 10-point threshold for substantial clinical improvement. A higher proportion of upper-level injuries in the control arm could partly explain the SCIM difference through respiratory-management scores; riluzole recipients also had a significant self-care-score change. Pre-planned subgroup analyses indicated neurological and functional improvements with riluzole in each AIS-grade subgroup. AIS A participants had greater mean neurological-level gain with treatment. For AIS B, the authors describe statistically superior baseline-to-180-day changes in SCIM, EQ5D health status, and SF-36 mental scores with riluzole. In AIS C, multivariate models found statistically significant greater Upper Motor and Total Motor change at 180 days, but no significant change in total SCIM score. Motor and functional gains tended to be greater with incomplete cervical injury, AIS grades B and C. The authors hypothesize either that limited regeneration after severe AIS A injury restricts the usefulness of neuroprotection or that motor and functional scales are insufficiently sensitive in AIS A. The AIS A neurological-level subgroup comparison was 0.50 versus 0.12 for placebo at 180 days (p: 0.077). Figure 2 depicts secondary outcomes by baseline AIS subgroup in the CC population (n: 137); Figure 3 depicts post hoc regression of motor-score changes, adjusted for age, Charlson comorbidity Index, gender, neurological level of injury, and race, also in the CC cohort (n: 137). The authors discuss a separate riluzole pharmacodynamics investigation that associated treatment with reduced phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain (pNF-H), described as an axonal-degradation biomarker, versus placebo. Its three-dimensional pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic models also associated higher riluzole concentrations with better neurological recovery after 6 months. The trial illustrates the need for a minimally clinically important difference (MCID) suitable for tSCI trial end-points. Its power calculations assumed a change of 9 total motor score; the authors state that later thinking favors a lower MCID, closer to changes observed here. Some regard any neurological change as clinically important, whereas distribution-based analyses have estimated an MCID of 5 total motor scores. The authors suggest that future trials might place greater emphasis on functional primary outcomes such as SCIM because meaningful quality-of-life improvement may not appear in total motor scores. They call for more investigation of neuroprotective and regenerative agents' effects on function and rehabilitation. Given limitations of acute neurological examinations and difficulty defining a broadly applicable MCID, they suggest objective imaging and chemical markers such as pNF-H may better indicate recovery, while emphasizing the need to validate such biomarkers. A major trial limitation was recruitment of only 55% of the planned sample. The cohort also had predominantly severe AIS A and upper cervical injuries, which tend to have less recovery potential. Failure to meet recruitment targets qualifies interpretation of the prespecified superiority criterion. Primary, subgroup, and post hoc analyses nonetheless suggested possible neurological and functional recovery benefits that warrant consideration, without establishing definitive riluzole efficacy. Because similarly large tSCI trials are difficult, the authors propose that guideline committees review RISCIS findings to clarify riluzole's possible role. They consider its observed safety profile favorable but do not make a definitive efficacy claim. They argue that, with no accepted effective pharmacological neuroprotective or neuroregenerative treatment for this uncommon orphan disorder, a higher false-positive probability might be considered more acceptable when evaluating possible neurological benefit. The urgency, heterogeneity, and relative rarity of SCI complicate trials, as do comparable features of other neurological disorders. The authors cite advocacy proposals for Duchenne muscular dystrophy and ALS trials involving virtual controls, greater use of secondary outcomes, and possible removal of placebo arms. They also suggest more personalized, patient-centered outcomes and designs. Multi-arm, multi-stage (MAMS) platforms used in rare diseases and oncology might reduce tSCI trial costs and recruitment demands; analogous platforms have been proposed for Parkinson’s disease and ALS (ClincalTrials.gov NCT04302870).

document_sections.heading: Transparency, Rigor, and Reproducibility Summary
document_sections.content: The protocol and analysis plan were registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01597518) on May 14th, 2012. The specified sample size was 156 per group, providing power of 0.90 to detect an effect size of 9 in total motor score change. Block randomization assigned participants to riluzole or placebo, producing groups without baseline-characteristic differences. Study medication was received by 96 participants; the summary reports primary-outcome assessment in 68 after nine deaths and 28 incomplete assessments. Blinded investigators assessed all primary outcomes and could not identify treatment assignment more accurately than chance. Materials needed for treatment were widely available, and the primary outcome and main eligibility criteria were established tSCI standards. At interim analysis, the adaptive design changed from the original sequential approach to a non-binding futility hypothesis, with corresponding changes to superiority and futility thresholds. Findings had not been replicated or externally validated. The investigators state that de-identified individual participant data underlying the reported results and the protocol would be available through the corresponding author.

document_sections.heading: Data Sharing
document_sections.content: Subject to reuse conditions, the investigators planned to share de-identified individual participant data underlying the article's text, tables, figures, and appendices, together with the protocol, for individual participant data meta-analysis. Proposals could be submitted up to 36 months after publication. A committee of RISCIS investigators would review requests, and approved requestors would need a data access agreement.
